title: Dictionaries & Sets
summary: Key-value lookups with dicts, and unique collections with sets.

checkpoints.title: Dicts and sets
checkpoints.content: A dictionary, `person = {"name": "Ada", "age": 30}`, maps keys to values — `person["name"]` gets `"Ada"`. A set, `unique = {1, 2, 2, 3}`, automatically drops duplicates, ending up as `{1, 2, 3}` — sets have no guaranteed order and no key-value pairing.
checkpoints.explanation: Both use curly braces, but a dict always has `key: value` pairs while a set is just a collection of unique values.

hints.H0: Dicts use `key: value` syntax; sets are just comma-separated values.
hints.H1: Duplicate values in a set literal collapse down to one.
hints.H2: person["name"] looks up the value stored under that key.

checkpoints.title: Predict a dict lookup

options.explanation: .get(key, default) returns the default value when the key isn't found, instead of raising an error.
That's what scores["linus"] (square brackets) would do — .get() is specifically the safe alternative that doesn't raise.
None is only the default when you don't supply one yourself — here 0 was explicitly given as the fallback.

checkpoints.explanation: .get(key, default) looks up the key and falls back to the provided default (0 here) if it's missing, rather than raising.

hints.H0: "linus" isn't one of the keys in the dictionary.
hints.H1: .get() takes a second argument specifically for this situation.

checkpoints.title: Write a dict literal
checkpoints.content: Write a dictionary literal named `book` with exactly one key `"title"` mapped to the value `"Dune"`.
checkpoints.explanation: A dict literal pairs each key with its value using a colon, all inside curly braces.

hints.H0: Curly braces hold the key-value pairs.
hints.H1: Separate the key and value with a colon.

checkpoints.title: Predict a set's contents

options.explanation: Sets only keep unique values — every duplicate collapses down to a single occurrence.
A set can never contain duplicate values — that's its defining feature.

options.text: It raises an error because of the repeated values
options.explanation: Duplicates aren't an error for set() — they're just silently removed.

checkpoints.explanation: Converting a list to a set automatically discards duplicate values, keeping each unique value exactly once.

hints.H0: This is the entire reason sets exist — think about what makes them different from lists.
hints.H1: Count how many distinct values are in the original list.
